topics.title: Reactance and impedance
topics.summary: Capacitors and inductors resist AC by an amount that depends on frequency; combine that with resistance as phasors, not plain numbers.

lensNotes.circuit: X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls with frequency, so capacitors pass high frequencies; X_L = 2πfL rises, so inductors block them. Impedance extends Ohm's law to AC: V = I·Z.
lensNotes.math: Impedance is a complex number: Z = R + jX, where the reactance X is +X_L for an inductor and −X_C for a capacitor. Magnitudes combine like the sides of a right triangle, |Z| = √(R² + X²), and the phase angle is atan(X/R): positive for an inductor, negative for a capacitor.
lensNotes.signals: Because X depends on frequency, every RC or RL network treats different frequencies differently, which is what makes filters. The phase shift between current and voltage is the signal lens on the same fact.

prerequisiteNotes.series_parallel: Impedances combine in series and parallel with the same rules as resistances, just with complex numbers.
prerequisiteNotes.rc_time_constant: A capacitor's reactance, 1/(2πfC), is why an RC circuit behaves differently at different speeds.

goals: Find the reactance of a capacitor or an inductor at a given frequency, and say which way it moves when the frequency changes
Combine a resistance and a reactance in series into an impedance magnitude and phase angle, and use I = V/|Z| to find the current
Explain why a capacitor's current leads its voltage by 90° and an inductor's current lags by 90°
Predict how a series RC or RL circuit behaves at DC, at very high frequency, and in between
topics.intuition: For a steady sine wave, a capacitor opposes current less as the frequency rises and an inductor more. Because a reactance's current and voltage peak a quarter cycle apart, in series it combines with resistance like the sides of a right triangle, not like plain numbers.
topics.why: A capacitor's current is i = C·dv/dt: it flows only while the voltage is changing. At twice the frequency and the same amplitude, the voltage changes twice as fast, twice the current flows, and X_C = 1/(2πfC) halves. An inductor's voltage is v = L·di/dt, so the same current at a higher frequency takes more voltage: X_L = 2πfL rises. For a sine, the rate of change is largest at the zero crossings, so a capacitor's current peaks a quarter cycle before its voltage and an inductor's a quarter cycle after. That 90° offset is why reactance and resistance cannot simply be added.
topics.explanation: In a resistor, Ohm's law sets the current: I = V/R. With a sine wave, a capacitor or an inductor also limits the current, by an amount that depends on frequency: its reactance, X, in ohms. A capacitor's is X_C = 1/(2πfC): infinite at DC (an open circuit) and falling toward zero as the frequency rises. An inductor's is X_L = 2πfL: zero at DC (just a wire) and rising with frequency. With ω in rad/s instead of f in hertz, they are 1/(ωC) and ωL. Reactance differs from resistance in timing. In a resistor, current and voltage peak together. In a capacitor the current peaks a quarter cycle (90°) before the voltage; in an inductor, 90° after. So a resistance and a reactance in series add like the sides of a right triangle: |Z| = √(R² + X²). This is the impedance, and Ohm's law carries over as I = V/|Z|. The phase angle of a series RL is +atan(X_L/R), the voltage leading the current; of a series RC, −atan(X_C/R), the voltage lagging. As complex numbers, Z = R + jX_L or R − jX_C, and impedances combine by the same rules as resistances.

workedExample.problem: A 5 V (amplitude) sine at 1 kHz drives a 1 kΩ resistor in series with a 100 nF capacitor. Find the capacitor's reactance, the impedance and its phase angle, the current, and the voltage across each part. Then find the current at 10 kHz.
steps: φ = −atan(X_C/R) = −atan(1.59 kΩ / 1 kΩ) = −57.9°: the voltage across the pair lags the current by 57.9°.

V_R = I·R = 2.66 mA × 1 kΩ = 2.66 V and V_C = I·X_C = 2.66 mA × 1.59 kΩ = 4.23 V. They add to 6.89 V as plain numbers, more than the 5 V supply, but they peak 90° apart: √((2.66 V)² + (4.23 V)²) = 5.00 V.

At 10 kHz: X_C = 1/(2π × 10 kHz × 100 nF) = 159 Ω, |Z| = √((1 kΩ)² + (159 Ω)²) = 1.01 kΩ, and I = 5 V / 1.01 kΩ = 4.94 mA. Ten times the frequency raised the current by less than 2×, because the resistor now sets most of the impedance.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "AC capacitor circuits"
sources.note: A capacitor passes current in proportion to dv/dt, so its current leads its voltage by 90° and X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(ωC) falls as frequency rises.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 3 "Reactance and Impedance -- Inductive", section "AC inductor circuits"
sources.note: An inductor drops voltage in proportion to di/dt, so its current lags its voltage by 90° and X_L = 2πfL = ωL rises with frequency.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "Series resistor-capacitor circuits"
sources.note: In a series RC circuit, Z = R − jX_C, so |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) at a negative angle of arctan(X_C/R), with the source voltage lagging the current, and I = V/Z.

templates.prompt: What is the reactance of a {C} capacitor at {f}?
templates.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(2π × {f} × {C}) = {answer}. Double the frequency and the reactance halves.
hints: Capacitive reactance falls as frequency rises.

misconceptions.feedback: That's 2πfC (the susceptance, in siemens). Reactance is its reciprocal: X_C = 1/(2πfC).

followUps.prompt: Why does a capacitor's reactance fall as the frequency rises?

choices.text: Its current is set by how fast its voltage changes (i = C·dv/dt), and a higher frequency changes it faster
choices.feedback: Right: each half cycle moves the same charge, C times the voltage swing, but in less time, so more current flows for the same voltage.

choices.text: The capacitance grows at high frequency
choices.feedback: C is fixed by the plates and the dielectric. What changes is how often that charge is moved.

choices.text: Charge leaks straight through the dielectric at high frequency
choices.feedback: No charge crosses an ideal dielectric at any frequency. Current flows in the wires as the plates fill and empty; the faster they alternate, the more current.

choices.text: The capacitor stays fully charged, so it stops opposing the current
choices.feedback: The opposite: at high frequency it never has time to charge much, so it builds up little voltage to oppose the current.

followUps.explanation: Every half cycle the plates take on a charge Q = C·V and give it back. At twice the frequency the same charge moves in half the time: twice the current for the same voltage, so half the reactance. At DC nothing moves once the capacitor is charged, so X_C is infinite. This is why a capacitor "passes" high frequencies and blocks DC.

templates.noDrawing: the reactance of a single capacitor at a frequency; no circuit

templates.prompt: What is the reactance of a {L} inductor at {f}?
templates.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = 2π × {f} × {L} = {answer}. Inductive reactance grows with frequency.

misconceptions.feedback: That's the capacitor's form. For an inductor, X_L = 2πfL: higher frequency, more reactance.

templates.noDrawing: the reactance of a single inductor at a frequency; no circuit

templates.prompt: A {R} resistor is in series with a {C} capacitor. What is the magnitude of their impedance at {f}?
templates.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC) = {Xc}. Resistance and reactance are 90° apart, so they combine like a right triangle: |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) = √({R}² + {Xc}²) = {answer}.

misconceptions.feedback: R and X_C are 90° out of phase, so they don't add directly. Use |Z| = √(R² + X_C²).

followUps.prompt: Why is |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) and not simply R + X_C?

choices.text: The voltages across R and C peak a quarter cycle apart, so their peaks never add
choices.feedback: Right: V_R is in step with the current and V_C lags it by 90°. The total is their phasor sum, the long side of a right triangle.

choices.text: X_C isn't in ohms, so it can't be added to R
choices.feedback: X_C is in ohms: I·X_C gives the capacitor's voltage amplitude. The problem is timing, not units.

choices.text: The capacitor's reactance is negative, so it partly cancels R
choices.feedback: In complex form the capacitor's part is indeed −jX_C, but the j puts it at right angles to R, so it can't cancel it. Opposite reactances cancel (a capacitor against an inductor); R and X_C add at right angles, like the two short sides of a right triangle. |Z| is bigger than either but smaller than their sum.

choices.text: The capacitor wastes some energy, which makes the total smaller
choices.feedback: An ideal capacitor wastes nothing; it stores energy and gives it back. The smaller total comes from timing.

followUps.explanation: The same current flows through both parts. v_R peaks with the current; v_C peaks a quarter cycle later. Their amplitudes are I·R and I·X_C, and two sines 90° apart add to a sine whose amplitude is √(V_R² + V_C²), not V_R + V_C. Divide by I and you get |Z| = √(R² + X_C²). It's the series rule from Series and parallel resistance, with phase included.

templates.prompt: A {R} resistor in series with a {C} capacitor is driven at {f}. What is the phase of the voltage across the pair relative to the current, in degrees? Give the sign: negative means the voltage lags (a capacitor alone would be −90°).
templates.explanation: φ = −atan(X_C/R) = −atan({Xc}/{R}) = −atan({ratio}) = {answer}. The capacitor makes the voltage lag the current (by 90° for a capacitor alone, 0° for a resistor alone).
hints: The phase is the angle of Z = R − jX_C.

misconceptions.feedback: That's in radians. Multiply by 180/π for degrees.
The ratio is upside down: use atan(X_C/R), with X_C = 1/(2πfC).

templates.prompt: A {V} (amplitude) sine at {f} drives a {R} resistor in series with a {L} inductor. What is the current amplitude?
templates.explanation: X_L = 2πfL = {XL}. |Z| = √(R² + X_L²) = {Z}. Ohm's law for AC: I = V/|Z| = {V}/{Z} = {answer}.

misconceptions.feedback: The inductor adds reactance at AC: divide by |Z| = √(R² + X_L²), not by R alone.
R and X_L are 90° apart, so combine them as √(R² + X_L²), not R + X_L.

templates.prompt: How does an ideal capacitor behave at DC and at very high frequency?

choices.text: Open circuit at DC, nearly a short at very high frequency
choices.feedback: Yes: X_C = 1/(2πfC) is infinite at f = 0 and tends to 0 as f grows.

choices.text: Short at DC, open at very high frequency
choices.feedback: That's the inductor. A capacitor blocks DC (once charged, no current flows).

choices.text: The same at all frequencies
choices.feedback: Only a resistor is frequency-independent. X_C falls as frequency rises.

choices.text: Open at both
choices.feedback: At high frequency the plates charge and discharge so fast that current flows almost freely: X_C → 0.

templates.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC): infinite at DC (open circuit), and tiny at high frequency (nearly a short). Inductors do the opposite: X_L = 2πfL.
templates.noDrawing: a conceptual question about any capacitor; no specific circuit

templates.prompt: In a capacitor driven by a sine wave, how are the current and voltage related in time?

choices.text: The current leads the voltage by 90°
choices.feedback: Yes: i = C·dv/dt, and the derivative of a sine is a cosine, a quarter period ahead.

choices.text: The voltage leads the current by 90°
choices.feedback: That's the inductor: v = L·di/dt, so its voltage peaks when the current changes fastest, a quarter period before the current peaks.

choices.text: They're in phase
choices.feedback: That's a resistor. A capacitor's current follows the rate of change of voltage.

choices.text: They're 180° apart
choices.feedback: 180° would be an inverted copy. A capacitor shifts by a quarter period.

templates.explanation: i = C·dv/dt: the current is largest when the voltage is changing fastest (at its zero crossings), so the current peaks a quarter period before the voltage.
templates.noDrawing: a conceptual question about any capacitor; no specific circuit

templates.prompt: A {C} capacitor is driven at {f}. The frequency is raised to {new_f}. What happens to its reactance?

feedback.up: That's an inductor (X_L = 2πfL). A capacitor's current follows how fast its voltage changes, so a faster signal drives more current: less reactance.
feedback.same: Only a resistor ignores frequency. A capacitor's current follows how fast its voltage changes, i = C·dv/dt, and the same amplitude at a higher frequency changes faster, so the ratio of voltage amplitude to current amplitude, X_C = 1/(2πfC), depends on f.

templates.explanation: X_C = 1/(2πfC), so X_C goes as 1/f. Twice the frequency moves the same charge in half the time, which gives twice the current for the same voltage: {before} → {after}.
hints: Does a capacitor pass high frequencies or block them?

templates.prompt: A {V} (amplitude) sine at {f} drives a {R} resistor in series with a {C} capacitor. The frequency is raised to {new_f}, with the same amplitude. What happens to the current?

feedback.down: A higher frequency doesn't make a capacitor oppose the current more: X_C = 1/(2πfC) shrinks as f rises, and |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) follows it.
feedback.same: R doesn't change, but X_C = 1/(2πfC) does, and |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) includes it.

whatIf.factorHint: X_C = 1/(2πfC) follows 1/f, but R doesn't change with frequency, and |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) includes both. Work out |Z| before and after; the current is V/|Z|.

templates.explanation: X_C falls from {Xc} to {Xc2}, so |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) falls and I = V/|Z| rises: {before} → {after}. It rises by less than ×10, because R doesn't shrink: as X_C gets small, R alone limits the current.
hints: What happens to X_C? Then to |Z| = √(R² + X_C²)?

templates.prompt: A series RC network is driven by a {f} sine. The voltage across the pair must lag the current by {phi}° (within 5% of {phi}°). Choose R (1 kΩ to 100 kΩ) and C (1 nF to 10 µF), both standard E12 values.
templates.explanation: The angle of Z = R − jX_C is set by the ratio of its sides: the voltage lags by atan(X_C/R). For {phi}° you need X_C/R = tan {phi}° = {ratio}. With R = 10 kΩ, X_C must be {Xc1}, so C = 1/(2π × {f} × X_C) = {Cex}. Round C to E12 and check the angle; if it is outside 5%, try a neighboring R. Scaling R up and C down by the same factor multiplies X_C and R alike, so the ratio, and the angle, stay put: many pairs work.
hints: What sets the angle: the sizes of R and X_C, or their ratio?
tan φ = X_C/R. Pick R, find the X_C you need, then C = 1/(2πf·X_C).

followUps.prompt: A 1 kΩ design and a 100 kΩ design can give the same phase angle at {f}. Why?

choices.text: The angle depends only on the ratio X_C/R, so scaling R up and C down by the same factor leaves it unchanged
choices.feedback: Right: a hundred times the R with a hundredth of the C gives a hundred times the X_C too, so X_C/R and the angle stay the same.

choices.text: The angle depends only on the capacitor, so R can be anything
choices.feedback: Change R alone and X_C/R changes, and so does the angle: a bigger R lets the resistor dominate and pulls the angle toward 0°.

choices.text: Both designs have the same impedance magnitude |Z|
choices.feedback: |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) is a hundred times bigger in the 100 kΩ design. Only the shape of the R–X_C triangle is the same, not its size.

choices.text: The angle depends only on the frequency
choices.feedback: The frequency sets X_C for a given C, but the angle comes from X_C compared with R. At the same frequency, a different X_C/R gives a different angle.

followUps.explanation: R and X_C are the two short sides of a right triangle, and the phase is its angle, set by the ratio of the sides. Multiply R by 100 and divide C by 100: X_C = 1/(2πfC) also grows 100 times, so the triangle is the same shape, only bigger. The current is a hundred times smaller; its timing against the voltage is unchanged.

templates.prompt: A function generator (treat it as ideal) drives a {V} peak sine at {f} into R = {R} in series with C = {C}. A current probe reads the current through R, and a scope probe reads the voltage across C, both peak to peak. Healthy, the scope would show {h1} peak to peak across C. The readings are below. Which fault explains them?

probes.label: Current through R (current probe, peak to peak)
Voltage across C (scope, peak to peak)

faults.feedback: With C open, no current could flow, so the current probe would read 0 A. R, carrying nothing, would drop nothing, and the scope would show the generator's full {Vpp} peak to peak across the gap.
faults.why: No current flows, yet the scope shows the generator's whole {Vpp} peak to peak across C. R drops nothing because it carries nothing, so all of the voltage appears across the capacitor's position: the loop is broken there, and C is open.

faults.text: C is shorted (a cracked ceramic that failed short)
faults.feedback: With C shorted, the scope would read 0 V across it, and R alone would limit the current: 2 × {V}/{R} = {Ishort} peak to peak, more than the healthy {h0}.
faults.why: Current flows, more than healthy, yet C shows no voltage at all. The current is {V}/R in amplitude, {Ishort} peak to peak, set by R alone. A capacitor that carries current with no voltage across it has no reactance left: it is shorted.

faults.text: C is a tenth of its value ({Csmall} fitted in its place)
faults.feedback: A tenth of the capacitance would make X_C ten times larger, {Xcs}. |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) would rise, so the current would fall well below {h0}, and the capacitor, now most of the impedance, would take most of the generator's voltage: more than the healthy {h1}.
faults.why: The current fell, but not to zero, while the voltage across C rose toward the generator's {Vpp}. Divide one by the other: V_C/I is about {Xcs}, ten times the healthy X_C of {Xc}. X_C = 1/(2πfC) grows as C shrinks, so a capacitor a tenth of the value was fitted.

faults.text: R is ten times its value ({Rbig}: an orange multiplier band instead of red)
faults.feedback: With R ten times larger, |Z| would rise and the current would fall well below {h0}. X_C would be unchanged, so the capacitor's voltage, I·X_C, would fall in the same proportion, below the healthy {h1}.
faults.why: The current fell, and the voltage across C fell in the same proportion: V_C/I is still the healthy X_C of {Xc}. The capacitor is fine, so the extra impedance is resistance: R is too large.

faults.feedback: With R open, no current could flow, and nothing would reach the capacitor: the scope would show 0 V across it.
faults.why: No current, and no voltage across C either: nothing reaches the capacitor. The break is ahead of it, in R.

templates.explanation: Healthy, X_C = 1/(2πfC) = {Xc}, and the impedance is |Z| = √(R² + X_C²) = {Z}, so the current is 2 × {V}/{Z} = {h0} peak to peak and the capacitor shows I·X_C = {h1}. Read the faulty circuit the same way. No current means the loop is open somewhere; the scope then tells you where: the full {Vpp} across C means C is open, 0 V means the break is ahead of it, in R. Current with no voltage across C means C is shorted. When both readings are nonzero but wrong, divide the capacitor's voltage by the current: that is X_C as the circuit sees it. Ten times {Xc} means a capacitor a tenth of the value; an unchanged X_C with less current means the extra impedance is resistance.
hints: Is any current flowing? If not, does the capacitor show the full generator voltage or none?
If both readings are nonzero, divide the capacitor's voltage by the current and compare it with the healthy X_C = 1/(2πfC).
